Victory and Its Judgment

Nuremberg and the United Nations

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

When the guns stopped, the winners faced two questions. What should be done with the men who had ruled Germany and Japan? And what could keep a third great war from coming? This lesson looks at the trial at Nuremberg and at the founding of the United Nations. Both rested on the hope that law could do what force alone had failed to do. Keep that hope in mind when you read a primary source in this module.

Objectives
  1. Explain why the Allies tried the Nazi leaders at Nuremberg and what the main charges were.
  2. Describe the objections to the trial and how the court answered them.
  3. Describe how the United Nations was set up and how it differed from the League of Nations.
Quick Check-in

Victorious nations try the leaders of their defeated enemy. What do you think would make such a trial fair?

The Book
Parts 1 to 3
?
Historical Figure
Robert JacksonROB-ert JAK-sun

Robert Jackson (1892 to 1954) was a self-taught lawyer from upstate New York who never attended a full law school course. He served as Attorney General under Roosevelt, and in 1941 Roosevelt put him on the Supreme Court.

He took leave from the Court to lead the American prosecution at Nuremberg, and he shaped the case and the charter. He was a gifted speaker, and his opening speech is remembered as one of the best of the century. The work was hard, and it caused quarrels with the other prosecutors and with his own colleagues. He returned to the Court in 1946 and served until his death.

City
Nuremberg

Nuremberg is a city in Bavaria, in southern Germany, that was a great center of trade and craft in the Middle Ages. The Nazis chose it for their yearly party rallies, which drew hundreds of thousands, and in 1935 they announced the race laws there.

In January 1945 Allied bombers destroyed most of the old city. The Palace of Justice, a large courthouse on the edge of town, was damaged but could be repaired in a few months. The trial began in its largest courtroom in November 1945. The choice of the city was meant to show that the regime had ended where it had made its show of strength.

KatynA place in Russia where Soviet police shot thousands of Polish officers in 1940.

technicalityA small point of rule or procedure that decides a case instead of its main question.
tribunaltry-BYOO-nulA court set up to hear a special kind of case.
unconditional surrenderun-kun-DISH-un-ul suh-REN-derA surrender in which the defeated side gets no promises in return and accepts whatever terms the winner sets.
vetoVEE-tohThe power to block a decision by saying no.

Victory and Its Judgment

Nuremberg and the United Nations

Part 1

The Case for a Trial

Chapter 1Should There Be a Trial?
Chapter 2The Trial
Chapter 1

Should There Be a Trial?

Germany had given up by unconditional surrender on May 8, 1945. The Allies had warned since 1943 that they would punish war criminals, but they did not agree on how. Churchill at one time favored shooting the top Nazi leaders without a trial. The Soviets wanted a show of guilt. Many Americans, led by Secretary of War Henry Stimson, argued for a real trial with real evidence. They believed that a trial would give a permanent record of what had been done, and show the world that the winners were bound by law.

Truman agreed, and he chose a justice of the Supreme Court, Robert Jackson, to lead the American case. In August 1945 the four great powers, the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union, signed a charter in London for an International Military Tribunal. The trial was held in Nuremberg, because its Palace of Justice was still standing and had a prison attached. It was also the city where the Nazis had held their great rallies and passed their race laws.

Chapter 2

The Trial

The trial opened on November 20, 1945. Twenty-four men were named in the indictment, and twenty-two stood in court. Hitler, Himmler, and Goebbels were already dead, so the highest man in the dock was Hermann Göring. Four judges sat on the tribunal, one from each of the four powers, and each country had its prosecutors. The charges were four: a plot to wage war, crimes against peace, which meant starting an aggressive war, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.

Jackson’s opening speech on November 21 told the court why the trial mattered, and you will read part of it in this module. Most of the proof came from the Nazis themselves, in thousands of captured documents. On November 29 the court watched films of the camps, shot by Allied soldiers. The defendants were allowed lawyers, and they could call witnesses and question those who testified against them. Most of them said that they had only followed orders. The tribunal rejected that defense, though it allowed it to be weighed when deciding the sentence.

Part 2

The Objections and the Verdicts

Chapter 3The Objections
Chapter 4The Verdicts
Chapter 3

The Objections

The defense made two serious objections. The first was that the charge of crimes against peace was an ex post facto law, a law made after the act. The old rule nullum crimen sine lege says that no one may be punished for something that was not a crime when it was done. The tribunal answered that Germany had signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928, which gave up war as a way of settling quarrels, and that justice would be poorly served if the guilty went free on a technicality. Some American leaders, such as Senator Robert Taft, still thought the principle had been broken.

The second objection was that it was victors’ justice. The Soviet Union had joined Hitler in attacking Poland, and it had shot Polish officers at Katyn. The Soviet prosecutors tried to blame Katyn on the Germans, and the court did not accept it. The Allies had also bombed cities. A fair observer must grant that the tribunal was not perfect. But it heard evidence, and it gave every man a defense, which was more than the Nazis had given their victims.

Chapter 4

The Verdicts

The verdicts came on October 1, 1946. Twelve men were sentenced to death, three to life in prison, and four to shorter terms, and three were found not guilty. Göring took poison in his cell a few hours before he was to be hanged. The rest of the condemned were executed on October 16. Later American courts at Nuremberg tried doctors, judges, and business leaders. In Tokyo a similar tribunal tried Japan’s leaders from 1946 to 1948, and seven men, among them Hideki Tojo, were hanged. In its judgment the Nuremberg tribunal said that crimes are committed by men and not by abstract entities, and that a person has duties that go beyond obedience to his own state. These trials set a principle that leaders can be held to account for crimes against peace and humanity, though many of the same questions about fairness came up there too.

Part 3

The United Nations

Chapter 5The United Nations
Chapter 6Law and the Strong
Chapter 5

The United Nations

The second hope was an organization to keep the peace. You have read how the League of Nations failed, partly because the American Senate refused to join. Roosevelt had planned a new body during the war, and in April 1945 delegates from fifty nations met in San Francisco to write its charter. It was signed on June 26. The Senate approved it on July 28 by a vote of 89 to 2, and it took effect on October 24, 1945.

All members sit in a General Assembly, but the real power lies in the Security Council. It has five permanent members, the United States, Britain, France, the Soviet Union, and China, and each holds a veto. Any one of them can block action. This was a price paid for the great powers’ membership, because they would not join otherwise. But it meant that the United Nations could not act against any of them. The founders were realistic about this, since they knew that peace could not be kept by a body that the strongest states would not obey.

Chapter 6

Law and the Strong

The Assembly also created agencies for food, health, and refugees, and in 1948 it adopted a Universal Declaration of Human Rights, though the declaration had no power to enforce itself. Look back at the two efforts of this lesson. Each tried to bind the strong to a rule of law, and each depended on the strong agreeing to be bound. As you read Jackson’s words in this module, ask whether law that rests on the consent of the powerful is a weakness or a beginning.
